terraform-aws.wrapped_text:
Terraform for AWS
The AWS provider lets Terraform
manage resources in Amazon Web
Services through the AWS APIs.
HashiCorp maintains it under the
source address `hashicorp/aws`
([provider docs](https://registry.
terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/a
ws/latest/docs)). A second
provider, `hashicorp/awscc`,
reaches AWS through the Cloud
Control API instead ([awscc docs](
https://registry.terraform.io/prov
iders/hashicorp/awscc/latest/docs)
). The [Terraform
map](../terraform.md) explains
Terraform itself.

The unit is one AWS account and
one region. Each provider block
reaches one account through a
chain of identities, and it works
in one region by default ([The
Identity Chain](#the-identity-chai
n-the-identity-chain)). AWS has
hundreds of services. A data
engineer meets a few of them:

- S3 buckets hold data files, such
as Iceberg tables and files for
Snowpipe.
- IAM roles and policies decide
who may read and write those
files. IAM is AWS Identity and
Access Management.
- Secrets Manager holds passwords
and keys for programs.
- SQS queues, SNS topics and
Lambda functions react to new
files.
- ECS services and RDS databases
run the apps that produce or serve
data.

Four ideas explain most AWS plans:

- Many AWS settings are one
document, such as the notification
settings of a bucket. Each
document can have only one owner
in Terraform ([One Document, One O
wner](#one-document-one-owner-one-
document-one-owner)).
- Some resources add one item to a
set, and others own the whole set
([Adders and Owners](#adders-and-o
wners-adders-and-owners)).
- Access between AWS and another
system needs trust on both sides
([Trust Has Two Sides](#trust-has-
two-sides-trust-has-two-sides)).
- Every value that Terraform reads
or writes, secrets included, sits
in the state ([State Holds Secret 
Values](#state-holds-secret-values
-state-holds-secret-values)).

Deletes also differ by service,
and each provider version changes
some rules ([Deletes Differ by Ser
vice](#deletes-differ-by-service-d
eletes-differ-by-service);
[Provider Generations](#provider-g
enerations-provider-generations)).

Now compare Snowflake. In
Snowflake, the role that creates
an object owns it, and grants
decide access. In AWS, the account
owns every resource, and IAM
policies decide access. A
Snowflake grant connects a role to
an object; an IAM policy connects
an identity to actions on
resources.

The map has four parts. Mental
Models explains the ideas above.
Reading an AWS Configuration says
what you will see and where to
look first. Pitfalls lists the
failures that experienced users
plan around. Good and Bad
Decisions compares the main design
choices.

- SQS queues, SNS topics and Lambda functions react to new files.

the-identity-chain.wrapped_text:
The Identity Chain
Terraform starts with some credentials, for
example the keys of a pipeline. The provider
can then assume an IAM role in the target
account with `assume_role`, and it can assume
several roles in a row ([role chaining](https:
//github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/
blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/index.html.markdown#
L77)). The final role decides which account
the plan touches and what it may do. So read
the `role_arn` expression of every provider
block. When it depends on the workspace, the
workspace picks the account.

Two settings help. `allowed_account_ids` stops
a run in the wrong account. `default_tags`
adds the same tags to every resource of the
provider ([provider arguments](https://github.
com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.7
3.0/website/docs/index.html.markdown#L372-L380
)). The backend that stores the state has its
own chain, set in the `backend "s3"` block.

A configuration can have several provider
blocks with aliases, for example one for a DNS
account and one for the region `us-east-1`. A
resource then picks its block with `provider =
aws.<alias>`.

one-document-one-owner.wrapped_text:
One Document, One Owner
Several AWS settings are a single document
that the API replaces as a whole:

- The notification configuration of an S3
bucket ([notification note](https://github.com
/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0
/website/docs/r/s3_bucket_notification.html.ma
rkdown#L13)).
- The lifecycle configuration and the policy
of a bucket.
- The access policy of an SQS queue or an SNS
topic.
- The inline rules of a security group, which
is a firewall for network traffic.

If two resources, or a resource and a person,
write the same document, each write removes
the other's part. Plans then show the same
change again and again. Give each document
exactly one owner in Terraform.

Since provider version 4, an S3 bucket has one
resource for each document:
`aws_s3_bucket_versioning`,
`aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration`,
`aws_s3_bucket_policy`,
`aws_s3_bucket_notification` and others
([version 4 upgrade](https://github.com/hashic
orp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/websit
e/docs/guides/version-4-upgrade.html.markdown#
L1324-L1335)).

adders-and-owners.wrapped_text:
Adders and Owners
IAM attaches policies to roles. Two styles of
resource do this:

- Adders add one item and leave the rest
alone. Examples are
`aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` and
`aws_iam_role_policy`.
- Owners own the whole set and remove items
that they do not list. Examples are the
`inline_policy` and `managed_policy_arns`
arguments of `aws_iam_role` ([role note](https
://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws
/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/iam_role.html.mar
kdown#L15)), and the `*_exclusive` resources.

One owner is a trap.
`aws_iam_policy_attachment` owns every
attachment of one policy across the whole
account ([warning](https://github.com/hashicor
p/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/
docs/r/iam_policy_attachment.html.markdown#L13
)). If another configuration attaches the same
policy elsewhere, the next apply detaches it
there. Use `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment`
instead.

trust-has-two-sides.wrapped_text:
Trust Has Two Sides
An IAM role has a trust policy. It names who
may assume the role, and it can demand an
external ID, a shared value that the caller
must present ([external ID](https://docs.aws.a
mazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common
-scenarios_third-party.html)). Another system
that uses the role, such as Snowflake or a
Kafka Connect connector, must know the role
ARN and the external ID. So each side needs
values from the other side.

When the other system generates its values,
someone must copy them into the trust policy,
for example in a second apply. When you choose
the external ID yourself and fix the role name
in advance, both sides know every value before
the first apply. AWS does not treat the
external ID as a secret. The [Snowflake map](.
./snowflake/terraform-snowflake.md#two-step-tr
ust-with-aws-two-step-trust-with-aws) shows
the three ways that configurations solve this
loop for Snowflake.

state-holds-secret-values.wrapped_text:
State Holds Secret Values
The state stores every attribute that
Terraform reads or writes, in plain text:

- `aws_iam_access_key` stores the secret key
of an IAM user ([access key doc](https://githu
b.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6
.73.0/website/docs/r/iam_access_key.html.markd
own#L77)).
- `aws_secretsmanager_secret_version` stores
the secret value.
- `aws_db_instance` stores the master
password.
- A data source that reads a secret stores it
too.

Write-only arguments, such as
`secret_string_wo` and `password_wo`, keep a
value out of the state. They need Terraform
1.11 or later ([secret version doc](https://gi
thub.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob
/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/secretsmanager_secret_
version.html.markdown#L15)). A program can
also read a secret at run time by its ARN, so
the value never passes through Terraform.

deletes-differ-by-service.wrapped_text:
Deletes Differ by Service
A destroy in the plan means different things
for different services:

| Resource | What a destroy does |
| --- | --- |
| `aws_s3_bucket` | Fails if the bucket holds
objects, unless `force_destroy` is true; then
it deletes all objects and versions first
([bucket doc](https://github.com/hashicorp/ter
raform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/
r/s3_bucket.html.markdown#L58)). |
| `aws_secretsmanager_secret` | Schedules the
secret for deletion after a recovery window,
30 days by default ([secret doc](https://githu
b.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6
.73.0/website/docs/r/secretsmanager_secret.htm
l.markdown#L44)). |
| `aws_db_instance` | Fails while
`deletion_protection` is on; otherwise it
takes a final snapshot unless
`skip_final_snapshot` is true ([db_instance do
c](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-prov
ider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/db_instan
ce.html.markdown#L332)). |
| `aws_kms_key` | Schedules the key for
deletion after a waiting period of 7 to 30
days ([key doc](https://github.com/hashicorp/t
erraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/doc
s/r/kms_key.html.markdown#L316)). |
| `aws_sns_topic_policy` | Resets the policy
to the default instead of deleting it
([provider code](https://github.com/hashicorp/
terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/internal/s
ervice/sns/topic_policy.go#L108-L122)). |

So `-` in a plan can mean "gone now", "gone in
30 days" or "reset".

provider-generations.wrapped_text:
Provider Generations
Each major version of the provider changed how
code looks:

| Version | Released | Main change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4.0.0 | 2022-02-10 | S3 bucket settings
moved into separate resources. |
| 5.0.0 | 2023-05-25 | Tag handling changed,
and old arguments were removed. |
| 6.0.0 | 2025-06-18 | Each resource can set
its own `region`. |

The upgrade guides list every change ([version
6 guide](https://github.com/hashicorp/terrafor
m-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/guide
s/version-6-upgrade.html.markdown)). HashiCorp
advises moving to the latest minor version
first, getting a clean plan, and only then
raising the major version ([upgrade steps](htt
ps://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-a
ws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/guides/version-6-
upgrade.html.markdown#L109-L116)).

`awscc` is generated from AWS CloudFormation
schemas. Every optional attribute in it is
also computed, so it cannot detect drift in
values that you did not set, and it ignores
`default_tags` ([awscc docs](https://github.co
m/hashicorp/terraform-provider-awscc/blob/v1.1
10.0/docs/index.md#L20-L26)). HashiCorp built
it to bring new AWS resources to Terraform
faster, and expects it to run next to
`hashicorp/aws` ([using both providers](https:
//github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/
blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/guides/using-aws-wit
h-awscc-provider.html.markdown)).

aws-where-to-look-first.wrapped_text:
Where to Look First
Read an AWS configuration in this order:

1. The `terraform` block: the backend, its key
and its lock setting, and the version of
`hashicorp/aws`. A committed
`.terraform.lock.hcl` tells you the exact
build.
2. Every `provider "aws"` block: the region,
the `assume_role` role ARN, aliases,
`allowed_account_ids` and `default_tags`.
Together they tell you where each resource
lands.
3. The inputs per environment: workspaces,
variable files or YAML files. The same code
can run in several accounts.
4. IAM: the trust policies, the external IDs,
the attachment style, and every IAM user with
an access key.
5. The data buckets: `force_destroy`,
versioning, expiry, notifications and
policies. Data loss and event wiring live
here.
6. The secrets: where each value comes from,
the recovery window and `prevent_destroy`.
7. The `lifecycle` blocks, and the `moved`,
`removed` and `import` blocks. They show what
Terraform will not touch and what moved.
8. The event paths: queue and topic policies,
dead-letter queues, and Lambda timeouts.
9. The lookups of other states, such as data
sources by name or tag, and SSM parameters.

aws-where-to-look-first.wrapped_original_text:
Where to Look First
Read an AWS configuration in this order:

1. The `terraform` block: the backend, its key and its lock setting, and the version of `hashicorp/aws`. A committed `.terraform.lock.hcl` tells you the exact build.
2. Every `provider "aws"` block: the region, the `assume_role` role ARN, aliases, `allowed_account_ids` and `default_tags`. Together they tell you where each resource lands.
3. The inputs per environment: workspaces, variable files or YAML files. The same code can run in several accounts.
4. IAM: the trust policies, the external IDs, the attachment style, and every IAM user with an access key.
5. The data buckets: `force_destroy`, versioning, expiry, notifications and policies. Data loss and event wiring live here.
6. The secrets: where each value comes from, the recovery window and `prevent_destroy`.
7. The `lifecycle` blocks, and the `moved`, `removed` and `import` blocks. They show what Terraform will not touch and what moved.
8. The event paths: queue and topic policies, dead-letter queues, and Lambda timeouts.
9. The lookups of other states, such as data sources by name or tag, and SSM parameters. They are the contracts between configurations.

Force Destroy Empties the Bucket

bucket first deletes every object and every

Versioning Cannot Be Turned Off
`Disabled` is valid only when a bucket is
created or imported. A change from `Enabled`
or `Suspended` to `Disabled` fails, because S3
cannot return a bucket to the unversioned
state ([versioning doc](https://github.com/has

site/docs/r/s3_bucket_versioning.html.markdown
#L103-L104)). Use `Suspended` instead. After
you first enable versioning, AWS advises
waiting 15 minutes before writes ([versioning 
doc](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-pr
ovider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/s3_buck
et_versioning.html.markdown#L17)).

database-versions-and-replacements.wrapped_text:
Database Versions and Replacements
With automatic minor upgrades on, AWS raises
the engine version of an RDS instance by
itself. A configuration that pins
`engine_version = "16.4"` then plans a
downgrade, and AWS rejects it. The provider
docs advise a version prefix, such as `"16"`,
in that case ([db_instance doc](https://github
.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.
73.0/website/docs/r/db_instance.html.markdown#
L342)). Other changes replace the instance:
for example `engine`, `username`, `db_name` or
`storage_encrypted`. Keep
`deletion_protection` on and a final snapshot
set.

one-notification-configuration.wrapped_text:
One Notification Configuration per Bucket
`aws_s3_bucket_notification` writes the whole
notification configuration of a bucket, so a
bucket can have only one such resource
([notification note](https://github.com/hashic
orp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/websit
e/docs/r/s3_bucket_notification.html.markdown#
L13)). A second resource, a console edit, or a
Snowflake pipe with auto-ingest overwrites the
others. S3 also rejects two rules with
overlapping prefixes or suffixes for the same
event type ([event filters](https://docs.aws.a
mazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/notificati
on-how-to-filtering.html)). To send one event
to several readers, send it to one SNS topic
or to EventBridge, and fan out from there.

queue-timeouts-and-policies.wrapped_text:
Queue Timeouts and Policies
When a Lambda function reads an SQS queue, AWS
advises a visibility timeout of at least six
times the function timeout ([Lambda with SQS](
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/s
ervices-sqs-configure.html)). For example, a
function with a 60-second timeout needs a
queue visibility timeout of at least 360
seconds. With 300 seconds, a slow batch can
reach a second reader before the first one
finishes. Two more traps:

- Creating or updating a queue with a queue
policy hangs unless the policy sets `Version =
"2012-10-17"` ([queue note](https://github.com
/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0
/website/docs/r/sqs_queue.html.markdown#L13)).
- A queue policy for SNS or S3 should name the
sender with the condition `aws:SourceArn`, so
no other topic or bucket can write to the
queue ([confused deputy](https://docs.aws.amaz
on.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.ht
ml)).

Lambda Zips Built at Plan Time
The data source `archive_file` builds the zip
file of a Lambda function during the plan
([archive provider](https://github.com/hashico

changes that pass through Terraform. The newer
argument `code_sha256` also catches code
changed outside Terraform ([function doc](http
s://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aw
s/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/lambda_function.
html.markdown#L715)).

deleted-principals-break-trust.wrapped_text:
Deleted Principals Break Trust
When IAM deletes a user or role that a trust
policy names, it replaces the ARN in the
policy with an internal ID. A new role with
the same name does not restore the trust,
because it has a new ID ([principals](https://
docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/refer
ence_policies_elements_principal.html)). So a
replaced role silently locks out the systems
that it trusted, and the systems that trusted
it. Trust policies that name temporary session
ARNs have the same weakness.

So a replaced role silently locks out the systems that it trusted, and the systems that trusted it. Trust policies that name temporary session ARNs have the same weakness.

secrets-in-state.wrapped_text:
Secrets in State
An access key, a secret value or a database
password in the state is readable by anyone
who can read the state bucket. A sensitive
mark only hides the value in plan output.
Three ways reduce the exposure: write-only
arguments, programs that read secrets at run
time by ARN, and roles instead of access keys.
An imported access key has no secret in the
state at all ([access key doc](https://github.
com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.7
3.0/website/docs/r/iam_access_key.html.markdow
n#L122)).

deleted-secrets-hold-names.wrapped_text:
Deleted Secrets Hold Their Names
A deleted secret waits in a recovery window,
30 days by default ([DeleteSecret](https://doc
s.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/apirefe
rence/API_DeleteSecret.html)). During that
time, a new secret with the same name fails
with "The secret is scheduled for deletion" ([
CreateSecret](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secr
etsmanager/latest/apireference/API_CreateSecre
t.html)). So a rename or a replacement of a
secret resource cannot reuse the name at once.
The recovery window is also the only way back
from a wrong destroy. `recovery_window_in_days
= 0` deletes with no recovery.
`prevent_destroy` stops the destroy in the
plan.

iam-size-limits.wrapped_text:
IAM Size Limits
The inline policies of one role can hold
10,240 characters in total, and one managed
policy can hold 6,144 ([IAM quotas](https://do
cs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/referen
ce_iam-quotas.html)). A role can have 20
attached managed policies by default, and 25
at most. A growing `for_each` that adds
statements can pass the plan and fail the
apply at one of these limits.

arguments for assuming a role in `backend

A security group with inline `ingress` or
`egress` blocks owns all its rules. Its next
apply removes rules that someone added by
hand, by script or from another configuration.
The provider warns against mixing inline rules
with separate rule resources ([security group 
note](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-p
rovider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/securi
ty_group.html.markdown#L13-L15)). Use one
separate resource for each rule, such as
`aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule`.

version-bugs.wrapped_text:
Version Bugs
Each provider release fixes bugs, and some
releases add them. For example, on versions
6.0 to 6.8, a tag change on `aws_ecs_service`
appeared in every plan, but the apply never
wrote it; 6.9.0 fixed it ([issue 43570](https:
//github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/
issues/43570)). A patch-level pin, such as `~>
6.8.0`, keeps such a bug. With no committed
lock file, a loose constraint such as `>=
6.5.0` installs each new major version as soon
as it appears. Commit the lock file, and raise
versions on purpose.

Roles Instead of Access Keys
An IAM user with an access key has a
long-lived secret, and Terraform stores it in
the state. A role gives temporary credentials,
and there is no secret to store. AWS
recommends temporary credentials for workloads
([IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.
com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html))
. Use access keys only for a system that
cannot assume a role, and plan their rotation.

A bucket for test files can use
`force_destroy`, so it is easy to remove. A
bucket with data that cannot be rebuilt should
keep `force_destroy` false and add `lifecycle
{ prevent_destroy = true }`. Versioning and
expiry rules for old versions then protect
against overwrites without growing the bucket
forever.

contracts-between-configurations.wrapped_text:
Contracts Between Configurations
One configuration can need a value that
another one created, such as a certificate ARN
or a queue ARN. Three ways exist:

- Copy the value by hand into variables. It is
simple, but the copy goes stale without
warning.
- Look the resource up by name or tag with a
data source. The name becomes the contract.
- Publish the value as an SSM parameter in one
configuration and read it with
`data.aws_ssm_parameter` in the other. The
parameter name becomes the contract, and a
change flows on the next plan.

The last two follow a change; the first one
does not.
